solution.concept_anchor: Article 105(3) codification gap post-44th Amendment
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option c is deceptive because the 44th Amendment did mandate codification, making students think Parliament has since codified privileges, when in fact no such legislation exists.
elimination_logic: Eliminate option (a): Article 105 governs Parliament; Article 194 governs state legislatures — they are parallel, not identical provisions.
Eliminate option (c): The 44th Amendment inserted a mandate for Parliament to define privileges by law, but Parliament has not enacted such a law — no codification exists.
Eliminate option (d): The pre-Amendment position references privileges co-extensive with the House of Commons as of 1950, not as they exist today.

Confirm option (b): Because no codifying law has been enacted, the pre-44th Amendment position — privileges as enjoyed by the House of Commons at the commencement of the Constitution — continues to apply by constitutional default.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The classic trap here is that students recall the 44th Amendment (1978) inserted Article 105(3)'s mandate for Parliament to define privileges and incorrectly assume Parliament has done so. In reality, Parliament has not enacted any such law in over 45 years. This means the pre-Amendment position — privileges co-extensive with the House of Commons as they stood in 1950 — still operates as a constitutional default. A candidate who partially knows this topic will pick option (c), confusing the constitutional mandate with its actual fulfilment.
solution.final_explanation:
Article 105 of the Constitution grants privileges to Parliament and its members. Before the 44th Constitutional Amendment (1978), Article 105(3) provided that parliamentary privileges would be the same as those enjoyed by the House of Commons of the UK Parliament at the commencement of the Constitution. The 44th Amendment changed this to say privileges shall be as Parliament may by law define — but Parliament has never enacted such a law.

• Option (a): Incorrect. Article 105 applies to Parliament; Article 194 is the parallel provision for state legislatures. They are structurally similar but constitutionally distinct.
• Option (b): Correct. Since no law has been enacted under Article 105(3), the pre-amendment House of Commons privileges (as of 1950) continue to apply as the operative default.
• Option (c): Incorrect. The 44th Amendment mandated codification but did not itself codify privileges, and Parliament has not fulfilled this mandate.
• Option (d): Incorrect. The reference point is the House of Commons position as of the Constitution's commencement in 1950, not the current UK position.

Value Addition:
• Article 122 bars courts from questioning the validity of parliamentary proceedings on grounds of alleged irregularity of procedure.
• The 44th Amendment was enacted under the Janata government and introduced several liberal provisions.
• The gap between constitutional mandate and parliamentary action on privilege codification is a frequently examined UPSC theme.

solution.concept_anchor: Sita Soren 2024 overruling PV Narasimha Rao on bribery immunity

statement_analysis.statement: Under Article 105(1), a Member of Parliament enjoys complete immunity from court proceedings for any speech made or vote cast inside the House, and this immunity cannot be overridden by any other provision of the Constitution.
statement_analysis.reason: While Article 105(1) does grant immunity for speech and votes inside Parliament, the Supreme Court in Sita Soren (2024) clarified that bribery for a vote/speech is NOT protected — so the immunity is not absolute in the sense that it cannot coexist with criminal liability for the bribe transaction itself.

statement_analysis.statement: In the Sita Soren case (2024), a seven-judge Constitutional Bench unanimously overruled the PV Narasimha Rao judgment, holding that acceptance of a bribe by a legislator for casting a vote is not protected by parliamentary privilege.
statement_analysis.reason: The 2024 Constitution Bench unanimously held that privilege protects Parliament's functioning, not individual corruption — thereby overruling the 1998 five-judge bench verdict.

statement_analysis.statement: The freedom of speech under Article 105(1) is subject to the reasonable restrictions enumerated under Article 19(2), just as the general freedom of speech under Article 19(1)(a) is so constrained.
statement_analysis.reason: Parliamentary speech under Article 105(1) is absolute and is explicitly independent of Article 19 — it is not subject to the reasonable restrictions under Article 19(2).

solution.strong_distractor: b — Option b (statements 1 and 3 only) is a strong distractor because a student who partially remembers the PV Narasimha Rao immunity rule may mark Statement 1 as correct, and the Article 19(2) link in Statement 3 sounds plausible to those who conflate general free speech with parliamentary free speech.
elimination_logic: Eliminate Statement 1: The claim that immunity 'cannot be overridden by any provision' is falsified by Sita Soren (2024) — bribery related to a vote attracts criminal liability despite Article 105(1).
Confirm Statement 2: The Sita Soren 7-judge bench (2024) unanimously overruled PV Narasimha Rao — this is the current legal position and is factually precise.

Eliminate Statement 3: Article 105(1) speech immunity is completely independent of Article 19 — it is not subject to Article 19(2) restrictions; the two provisions operate in entirely different spheres.
Only Statement 2 is correct — select option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 1 is a partial-truth trap. It accurately describes the general rule of Article 105(1) immunity but adds the phrase 'cannot be overridden by any provision' — which was the pre-2024 understanding but is now incorrect after Sita Soren. Statement 3 is a conflation trap — students who know both Article 19(1)(a) and Article 105(1) protect speech may assume they share the same restriction framework, when in fact parliamentary immunity is deliberately absolute and independent of Part III.
solution.final_explanation:
Article 105(1) grants Members of Parliament absolute immunity for speeches and votes inside the House. Unlike Article 19(1)(a), this immunity is not subject to reasonable restrictions — it operates as a special constitutional protection independent of Part III.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: While immunity for speech and votes is broad, the Supreme Court's 2024 Sita Soren ruling clarified that accepting a bribe linked to a parliamentary act is criminally prosecutable. The immunity protects the parliamentary act (voting/speaking), not the corrupt transaction (bribery) that precedes it. The phrase 'cannot be overridden by any provision' is therefore incorrect.
• Statement 2 — Correct: In Sita Soren v. Union of India (2024), a seven-judge Constitutional Bench unanimously overruled the 1998 PV Narasimha Rao decision. The court held that privilege exists to serve Parliament's collective functioning, not to immunize individual corruption.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: Parliamentary free speech under Article 105(1) is entirely separate from Article 19(1)(a) and is not subject to the grounds of restriction under Article 19(2). The two provisions operate in different constitutional domains.

Value Addition:
• The PV Narasimha Rao (1998) ruling had created a perverse incentive — members who voted after taking a bribe were immune, while those who took the bribe but abstained were not.
• Sita Soren (2024) resolved this anomaly by treating the bribe transaction as distinct from the parliamentary act.
• Article 105(2) extends immunity to parliamentary publications and committee proceedings.

solution.concept_anchor: Article 105(2) limits — authorized vs unauthorized publication

statement_analysis.statement: No court can question the validity of proceedings in Parliament, which means courts cannot scrutinize legislative debates, procedural irregularities, or the reasoning behind a legislative vote.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 122 bars courts from questioning the validity of parliamentary proceedings on grounds of procedural irregularity — this statement accurately reflects the scope of parliamentary immunity from judicial scrutiny.

statement_analysis.statement: Article 105(2) extends immunity to any publication relating to parliamentary matters, regardless of whether such publication was authorized by the House or not.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 105(2) protects only publications made under the authority of a House — unauthorized publications of parliamentary proceedings do not enjoy this immunity and can be subjected to legal proceedings.

statement_analysis.statement: A Member of Parliament cannot be prosecuted in any court for any act committed outside the House if that act is connected to or arises from the member's parliamentary duties.
statement_analysis.reason: Parliamentary privilege does not extend to acts committed outside the House even if related to parliamentary duties — a member can be criminally prosecuted for acts outside the House, as confirmed by the Sita Soren (2024) ruling.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option d (all three) is a strong distractor because Statement 1 is genuinely correct, and students who accept it may doubt themselves and choose 'all three incorrect' by over-applying the concept of limited parliamentary immunity.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: Article 122 does bar courts from scrutinizing legislative debates and procedural irregularities — this is a correct statement, so it does NOT belong in the 'incorrect' set.
Evaluate Statement 2: The extension to 'any publication regardless of authorization' is false — only authorized publications are protected; this statement IS incorrect.
Evaluate Statement 3: The claim that acts outside the House enjoy immunity if connected to parliamentary duties is incorrect — privilege applies to acts inside the House, not outside.
Statements 2 and 3 are incorrect — select option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 exploits a scope-extension trap. Students may recall that parliamentary publications are protected and assume this covers all publications connected to Parliament. The critical qualifier is 'authorization by the House' — only officially authorized publications enjoy absolute privilege. Unauthorized reporting, even if factually accurate, does not carry Article 105(2) immunity and may be actionable.
solution.final_explanation:
Article 105(2) grants immunity from court proceedings for things said or done in Parliament and for authorized publications. The scope of this protection is precise and not unlimited.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Article 122 explicitly bars courts from questioning proceedings in Parliament on grounds of alleged procedural irregularity — this is a well-established constitutional protection.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The immunity under Article 105(2) applies specifically to reports and papers published under the authority of a House. Unauthorized publications — even if reporting parliamentary events accurately — do not enjoy this protection. The House's authorization is the operative trigger.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: Parliamentary privilege is geographically and functionally bounded. It protects acts done within parliamentary proceedings, not acts outside the House merely because they have some nexus to parliamentary work. Criminal prosecution for extra-parliamentary acts remains fully available.

Value Addition:
• The Searchlight case (1959) was an early Supreme Court case that examined the conflict between parliamentary privilege over publications and the fundamental right to freedom of press.
• Publication of authorized parliamentary reports is absolutely privileged — no defamation suit lies against the publisher.
• A journalist who misrepresents parliamentary debates in a publication can face contempt proceedings even if not a member.

solution.concept_anchor: PV Narasimha Rao 1998 to Sita Soren 2024 judicial evolution
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option b swaps the bench sizes, making students who half-remember that the overruling bench was larger but confuse which case had which bench size choose incorrectly.
elimination_logic: Anchor on the earliest known event: The PV Narasimha Rao case involved the JMM bribery scandal that arose from the 1993 no-confidence motion, decided by the Supreme Court in 1998 — this is the starting point.
Eliminate options placing the 7-judge bench decision before the 5-judge bench decision — a larger bench overrules a smaller bench, so the 5-judge decision must precede the 7-judge decision.
Eliminate options that place the Sita Soren overruling before 2020 — the case arose from Jharkhand and reached the Supreme Court for Constitution Bench referral after 2014.
Confirm the sequence: 5-judge bench PV Narasimha Rao (1998) → 7-judge bench Sita Soren (2024) — option (a) is correct.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The temporal trap here is that students may confuse the bench sizes or the direction of overruling. Some candidates recall that 'the bigger bench overruled the smaller one' but may invert which case had which bench composition. Option (b) is specifically designed to exploit this — it assigns the 7-judge bench to PV Narasimha Rao and the 5-judge bench to Sita Soren, which reverses the actual constitutional history.
solution.final_explanation:
The judicial evolution of parliamentary privilege on bribery spans two landmark Supreme Court decisions separated by over two decades.

Correct chronological sequence:

1. PV Narasimha Rao vs. State (CBI/SPE) (1998): A 5-judge Constitutional Bench dealt with the JMM bribery scandal tied to the 1993 no-confidence motion. The majority held that members who voted — even for a bribe — were protected by Article 105(1); those who took bribes but did not vote were not protected. This created a perverse incentive.

2. Sita Soren vs. Union of India (2024): A 7-judge Constitutional Bench unanimously overruled PV Narasimha Rao. The court held that bribery for a vote or speech is not protected by privilege. The corrupt transaction (accepting the bribe) is distinct from the parliamentary act (voting/speaking).

Why other options fail:
• Option (b): Inverts the bench sizes — PV Narasimha Rao was 5-judge, Sita Soren was 7-judge.
• Option (c): Places the overruling decision (Sita Soren) before the original decision — logically impossible.
• Option (d): Incorrectly attributes a 9-judge bench to either case.

Value Addition:
• A larger Constitutional Bench can overrule a smaller bench's decision — this is the mechanism used in Sita Soren.
• The Sita Soren case arose from Jharkhand Mukti Morcha MLA Sita Soren allegedly taking a bribe to vote for an independent candidate in the 2012 Rajya Sabha election.
• Post-Sita Soren, MPs accused of bribery can be investigated by the CBI/ED without parliamentary immunity shielding them.

(b) 7-judge bench upholding immunity for members who voted (1998) → 5-judge bench overruling that position and removing immunity for bribery (2024)

(d) 9-judge bench on legislative bribery (1993) → 5-judge bench modifying that ruling in the context of no-confidence motions (1998)

solution.concept_anchor: Breach of privilege procedure and Speaker's role
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option b correctly matches the Privileges Committee and direct breach but swaps the Speaker's admission role with the House's final determination, which sounds plausible to students who think the Speaker decides finally.
elimination_logic: Anchor on List I item A: 'Direct breach of privilege' refers to an act against an individual member — this pairs with List II item 3 (an act obstructing a member in discharge of duties).
Anchor on List I item B: 'Constructive breach' is an act against the House as a body — this pairs with List II item 1 (an act obstructing the House in performing its collective functions).
Identify List I item C: The Speaker's admission role is limited — the Speaker decides only if a prima facie case exists; the final determination belongs to the House — pairs with List II item 4.
List I item D: The Privileges Committee investigates and reports but does not determine finally — pairs with List II item 2.
Correct matching: A-3, B-1, C-4, D-2 — option (d).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap trap is in the matching of C and D. Students may confuse whether it is the Speaker or the Privileges Committee that makes the 'prima facie' determination, and whether the House or the Committee delivers the final verdict. In reality: the Speaker decides prima facie admissibility; the Committee investigates and reports; the House decides finally. Options (b) and (c) are designed to exploit this three-step process confusion.
solution.final_explanation:
Breach of privilege follows a structured procedure in Parliament. Understanding each stage is essential for matching correctly.

Correct pairings:
• A — Direct breach (List I) → 3 (List II): A direct breach targets an individual member — obstructing them in the discharge of their duties as a member.
• B — Constructive breach (List I) → 1 (List II): A constructive breach targets the House as a collective body — any act that obstructs the House in performing its constitutional functions.
• C — Speaker's admission (List I) → 4 (List II): The Speaker's role is limited to deciding whether a prima facie case for breach exists. The Speaker does NOT decide the final outcome.
• D — Privileges Committee (List I) → 2 (List II): After the Speaker admits a motion, the Committee investigates, records evidence, and submits a report — but the final decision rests with the House.

Trap pairing: Students often conflate C and D — the Speaker and the Committee both play roles, but at different stages. The Speaker gates the process; the Committee investigates; the House decides.

Value Addition:
• The Speaker's decision to admit or reject a privilege motion is final and not subject to judicial review under Article 122.
• Each House has its own Privileges Committee — the Rajya Sabha equivalent is called the Committee of Privileges.
• Privilege motions must be raised at the earliest opportunity — delay weakens admissibility.

solution.concept_anchor: Contempt of Parliament broader than breach of privilege
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option a is a strong distractor because both A and R are factually true statements, leading students to assume they must be causally connected — but the reason given (contempt of court analogy) does not explain why Parliament is the sole judge of its contempt.
elimination_logic: Step 1: Is Assertion (A) correct? — Yes. Contempt of Parliament is indeed broader than breach of privilege; it covers any act lowering the House's dignity even without violating a specific privilege.
Step 2: Is Reason (R) correct? — Yes. Parliament is indeed the sole judge of its own contempt — no external authority, including courts, can interfere in how Parliament handles contempt matters.

Step 3: Does R causally explain A? — No. The fact that Parliament is the sole judge of its contempt is a consequence of parliamentary sovereignty, not the reason why contempt is broader than breach of privilege. The breadth of contempt arises from its definitional scope — it captures dignity-lowering acts not covered by specific privilege rules. Parliament being its own judge is a separate principle about adjudicatory authority, not about definitional scope.
Both A and R are correct but R does not explain A — select option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: This is a conflation trap. Assertion A (contempt is broader than breach) and Reason R (Parliament is the sole judge) are both true, and they both relate to contempt of Parliament. Students who see two true statements about the same concept reflexively mark option (a). However, R addresses who adjudicates contempt; A addresses what constitutes contempt — these are definitionally distinct propositions with no causal link between them.
solution.final_explanation:
Contempt of Parliament and breach of privilege are related but distinct concepts in parliamentary law.

Assertion (A) — Correct: Contempt is definitionally broader than breach of privilege. A specific privilege violation is always a contempt, but contempt can occur even without breaching any named privilege. For example, creating a disturbance in the public gallery, publishing a false account of debates, or showing disrespect to the House's authority constitutes contempt even if no identifiable privilege rule is breached.

Reason (R) — Correct: Parliament is indeed the sole judge of its own contempt. No court can substitute its judgment for Parliament's on whether a particular act amounts to contempt or what punishment should follow.

Causal relationship: R does NOT explain A. R is about the adjudicatory authority for contempt matters (Parliament alone decides). A is about the definitional scope of contempt (wider than privilege). These are two independent propositions — knowing that Parliament alone judges contempt does not tell us why contempt is defined more broadly than privilege.

Correct option: (b) — Both A and R are correct, but R is not the correct explanation of A.

Value Addition:
• Contempt of Parliament ≠ Contempt of Court — different bodies, different legal frameworks, different punishments.
• Misrepresenting parliamentary proceedings in media is a classic example of contempt without a specific privilege breach.
• The House can punish for contempt by reprimand, admonition, or imprisonment (till end of session).

solution.concept_anchor: Parliamentary punishment powers — imprisonment duration and expulsion limits

statement_analysis.statement: Parliament's power to imprison a member for breach of privilege is an inherent power, not derived from any statute.
statement_analysis.reason: Parliamentary powers of punishment — including imprisonment — are inherent privileges of the House, not created by any legislation.

statement_analysis.statement: A member expelled from the House by Parliament is constitutionally barred from contesting elections to that House.
statement_analysis.reason: Expulsion removes a member from the current House but does not create any constitutional disqualification from contesting future elections — an expelled member can immediately contest a by-election.

statement_analysis.statement: Imprisonment ordered by Parliament under its privilege powers cannot extend beyond the current session of the House.
statement_analysis.reason: Parliamentary imprisonment is session-bound — the House's power to detain a person lapses at the end of the session, and the imprisoned person must be released.

statement_analysis.statement: Courts can question the validity of a parliamentary expulsion order if the expelled member demonstrates that the procedure prescribed by the House's own rules was not followed.
statement_analysis.reason: Under Article 122 and the principle established in Tej Kiran Jain case, courts cannot question the validity of expulsion — it is an internal proceeding of Parliament beyond judicial scrutiny.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Option c (Only three) tempts students who correctly identify Statements 1 and 3 as true and then mistakenly accept Statement 2 or 4 as also correct because the rules about expulsion and judicial review sound authoritative.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: Parliament's punishment power (including imprisonment) is inherent — not statutory. This is correct.
Evaluate Statement 2: Expulsion removes from current membership but creates NO constitutional bar to re-election — this is incorrect, making the count drop.
Evaluate Statement 3: Session-bound imprisonment is a well-established rule — Parliament cannot detain beyond the current session. Correct.
Evaluate Statement 4: Courts cannot question expulsion validity (Tej Kiran Jain case, Article 122) — the claim that procedural violation opens judicial review is incorrect.
Only Statements 1 and 3 are correct — select option (b) 'Only two'.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 is a scope-extension trap — students who know expulsion is the severest punishment may assume it carries additional consequences like electoral disqualification. In fact, there is no such constitutional bar. Statement 4 exploits the broader rule that courts can review whether a privilege exists (they can) but not how Parliament exercised it — the specific claim about procedural violation inviting review contradicts the Tej Kiran Jain ruling.
solution.final_explanation:
Parliament's power to punish for breach of privilege is inherent and operates through a graduated scale: admonition, reprimand, imprisonment, and expulsion.

• Statement 1 — Correct: These punishment powers are inherent to Parliament as a sovereign legislative body — they do not derive from any enacted statute.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Expulsion removes a member from the current House but carries no constitutional disqualification from future elections. An expelled member may immediately contest a by-election for the same seat.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Parliamentary imprisonment is session-limited. The power to detain is tied to the House being in session — upon prorogation or adjournment sine die, all imprisoned persons under parliamentary order must be released.
• Statement 4 — Incorrect: The Supreme Court in Tej Kiran Jain confirmed that courts cannot examine the validity of parliamentary expulsion — Article 122 places internal proceedings beyond judicial review, even if procedural rules were allegedly not followed.

Only two statements (1 and 3) are correct.

Value Addition:
• Expulsion is constitutionally the most severe punishment but politically the most contested — several expulsions have been revoked by the same House after political realignments.
• The House can also 'admonish' (mild rebuke) or 'reprimand' (severe rebuke) without imprisonment.
• An expelled member can be re-elected and readmitted to the same House.

solution.concept_anchor: Freedom from arrest — civil cases only, 40-day rule
solution.strong_distractor: d — Option d is a strong distractor because it correctly identifies civil immunity but places the arrest during session (which is correct) while adding that the member must still appear for a court hearing — implying partial compliance — which misrepresents the law.
elimination_logic: Identify the type of case: The scenario involves a civil debt recovery suit — this is a civil case, not a criminal case or preventive detention.
Apply the 40-day rule: Session + 40 days before + 40 days after = protected period. The arrest during active session clearly falls within this window.
Eliminate option (a): Criminal immunity does not apply here — but the question is about a civil suit, so this option is irrelevant to the scenario.
Eliminate option (b): Preventive detention is explicitly excluded from this protection — but this is a civil debt case, not preventive detention.
Eliminate option (d): The member is not merely entitled to a hearing — the arrest itself is void and the member must be released unconditionally.
Confirm option (c): Arrest in a civil case during session is void — the member must be immediately released, and the court order cannot be enforced during the protected period.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The core trap is that candidates extend freedom from arrest to criminal cases. The scenario is deliberately constructed as a civil debt recovery matter to test precision. Many candidates who know 'members cannot be arrested' apply this broadly, missing the restriction that it covers ONLY civil cases. Option (d) partially acknowledges civil immunity but adds a procedural requirement (court appearance) that does not exist in law — this partial-truth distractor catches candidates who apply the principle correctly but then second-guess themselves.
solution.final_explanation:
Parliamentary freedom from arrest is a privilege that protects members from civil arrest during a constitutionally defined period — it does not provide blanket immunity.

Applicable principle: A Member of Parliament cannot be arrested in a civil case during the session of the House and for 40 days before and after the session. An arrest made in violation of this protection is void, and the member must be released immediately.

Mapping to the scenario: The arrest for civil debt recovery occurs during an active session — this falls squarely within the protected period. The civil nature of the case triggers the protection.

• Option (a): Incorrect. Criminal cases explicitly fall outside this protection — but this scenario involves a civil suit, making this option irrelevant.
• Option (b): Incorrect. Preventive detention is also excluded from this protection — but again, this is not a preventive detention case.
• Option (c): Correct. Civil arrest during session is void — the member must be released and cannot be detained until the protected period ends.
• Option (d): Incorrect. There is no residual obligation on the member to appear before the court during the protected period — the civil process is fully stayed.

Value Addition:
• Freedom from arrest in civil cases applies during session, 40 days before, and 40 days after — total protection window is session + 80 days.
• This protection does NOT apply to: criminal cases, preventive detention under any law, or cases involving breach of privilege.
• Upon arrest (even in civil case), the arresting authority must notify the Speaker/Chairman immediately.

(a) The member can claim immunity only if the arrest relates to acts committed outside Parliament — since this is a civil suit unconnected to parliamentary duties, the arrest can proceed.
(b) The member can be arrested because freedom from arrest under parliamentary privilege applies only to criminal cases, not civil disputes.
(c) The arrest is void — the member is entitled to freedom from arrest in civil cases during session and for 40 days before and after, and must be released immediately.
(d) The arrest can be executed but the member must be produced before a court within 24 hours, after which the court will stay further proceedings for the duration of the session.

solution.concept_anchor: Secret sitting initiation — minister or 25 members, Lok Sabha Rules
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option c is deceptive because students may assume that the Speaker, being the presiding authority over all parliamentary proceedings, can unilaterally order a secret sitting — whereas the Rules require either a ministerial motion or support of at least 25 members.
elimination_logic: Identify the category: The question asks which does NOT belong to valid grounds/triggers for parliamentary proceedings under inherent privilege.
Evaluate option (a): Excluding strangers (visitors and press) is an inherent parliamentary privilege — valid.

Evaluate option (b): A secret sitting can be initiated by a minister OR on the support of at least 25 members under Lok Sabha Rules — a single backbench member alone cannot unilaterally demand a secret sitting. This is the odd one out.
Evaluate option (c): The Speaker can ask strangers to withdraw — this is an exercise of the inherent right to exclude. Valid.
Evaluate option (d): Prohibition of publication during secret sitting is an exercise of parliamentary privilege. Valid.
Option (b) is the odd one out — a single non-ministerial member cannot unilaterally trigger a secret sitting.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The plausible-fabrication trap is in option (b): 'a single backbench member can demand a secret sitting' sounds like a democratic safeguard that Parliament might provide, but no such individual right exists. The Lok Sabha Rules require either a minister to move the motion or at least 25 members to support it — individual demand is not sufficient. Students who are unfamiliar with the specific threshold may accept option (b) as valid, thinking parliamentary rules empower individual members broadly.
solution.final_explanation:
Parliament's right to conduct secret sittings and exclude strangers is an inherent privilege — not derived from any specific constitutional article.

• Option (a): Valid trigger — the House has an inherent right to exclude strangers (including press and visitors) from its proceedings at any time and without giving reasons.
• Option (b): NOT valid — Under Lok Sabha Rules, a secret sitting can be initiated by a minister moving the appropriate motion, or if at least 25 members support the demand. A single backbench member acting alone cannot demand a secret sitting — this is the odd one out.
• Option (c): Valid trigger — the Speaker has the authority to direct strangers to withdraw as part of the exercise of the House's inherent privilege to control its own proceedings.
• Option (d): Valid consequence — during a secret sitting, publication of proceedings is prohibited, and any violation is punishable as contempt of Parliament.

Value Addition:
• The secret sitting power is an uncodified inherent privilege — it is not derived from Article 105 specifically.
• Proceedings of a secret sitting cannot be published even after the session ends unless the House resolves to lift the prohibition.
• The distinction between inherent privileges (uncodified) and statutory privileges (codified by law) is important for UPSC.

solution.concept_anchor: Committee privilege extends outside Parliament premises if authorized

statement_analysis.statement: A member of the public who gives evidence before a parliamentary committee and makes a defamatory statement about a private individual during that testimony enjoys the same absolute privilege as a Member of Parliament speaking in the House.
statement_analysis.reason: Evidence given before parliamentary committees is privileged — witnesses cannot be sued for statements made in their evidence. This protection extends to private citizens appearing before committees.

statement_analysis.statement: Parliamentary privilege attaches to proceedings of a committee only when the committee meets within the physical precincts of Parliament — meetings held outside Parliament's building cannot enjoy this protection.
statement_analysis.reason: Privilege extends to proceedings of committees meeting outside Parliament's premises provided the committee is acting under proper authorization from the House — physical location is not the determining factor.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option a (both correct) is a strong distractor because Statement 1 is correct and sounds surprising enough that students may accept Statement 2 as equally valid, since it seems like a reasonable spatial limitation on privilege.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: Witnesses before parliamentary committees receive absolute privilege — this is well established and extends the same protection as members enjoy on the floor of the House. Statement 1 is correct.

Evaluate Statement 2: The clause 'only within physical precincts' is a scope-limitation that does not reflect actual law. Privilege follows the committee's authorized activity, not its physical location. Statement 2 is incorrect.
Statement 1 correct, Statement 2 incorrect — select option (c).
Wait — the options are formatted as: (a) Both correct, (b) Both incorrect, (c) Statement 1 correct but Statement 2 incorrect, (d) Statement 1 incorrect but Statement 2 correct. Select (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 is a scope-extension trap. It imposes a geographical limitation on parliamentary privilege that does not exist in law. The actual rule is that privilege follows the authorization from the House — a committee authorized to sit outside Parliament (e.g., on a field visit to investigate a matter) still conducts privileged proceedings. Students who intuitively feel that 'Parliament's privilege must be inside Parliament' will incorrectly mark Statement 2 as correct.
solution.final_explanation:
Parliamentary committees enjoy the same privileges as the full House — this is a fundamental principle of parliamentary law.

• Statement 1 — Correct: A witness giving evidence before a parliamentary committee enjoys absolute privilege for statements made during that testimony. This is not limited to members — any person (including a private citizen) who appears before a committee and makes statements in evidence is protected from defamation suits. This privilege is necessary to ensure witnesses can give frank testimony.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Privilege is not geographically bounded by the physical location of Parliament's building. The operative condition is whether the committee is acting under proper authorization from the House. If a committee is authorized to meet in a state capital or on a field visit, its proceedings there are equally privileged. Physical location within Parliament's precincts is irrelevant.

Value Addition:
• A private individual who obstructs the work of a parliamentary committee can be punished for contempt of Parliament.
• Evidence given before committees is privileged — but knowingly false evidence can attract contempt proceedings.
• Joint Parliamentary Committees (JPCs) enjoy the same privilege status as standing committees.

solution.concept_anchor: MSM Sharma vs Krishna Sinha 1959 — first major privilege case
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option c is deceptive because it attributes this landmark ruling to the Searchlight case, which is closely related to the same press-privilege controversy and often cited alongside MSM Sharma — students familiar with both cases may confuse which one was the formal citation.
elimination_logic: Eliminate option (a): The Kihoto Hollohan case (1992) dealt with the anti-defection law under the Tenth Schedule — not parliamentary privilege over press publications.

Eliminate option (c): The 'Searchlight case' is a popular name associated with this controversy (involving the Searchlight newspaper), but the formal legal citation is MSM Sharma vs. Sri Krishna Sinha — the two refer to the same matter but the formal case name is what the blank requires.
Eliminate option (d): Raja Ram Pal vs. Speaker (2007) dealt with expulsion of members for cash-for-question scam — not the 1959 press privilege case.
Confirm option (b): MSM Sharma vs. Sri Krishna Sinha (1959) was the first major Supreme Court case directly addressing parliamentary privilege over press publications — option (b) is correct.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap trap here is between 'MSM Sharma vs. Sri Krishna Sinha' and 'the Searchlight case'. The Searchlight was the newspaper at the center of the controversy — the Bihar Legislative Assembly had taken action against the Searchlight newspaper for publishing expunged portions of a debate. The formal legal citation is MSM Sharma vs. Sri Krishna Sinha (1959). UPSC frequently tests whether candidates know formal case names versus popular names in parliamentary privilege jurisprudence.
solution.final_explanation:

• Option (a): Incorrect — Kihoto Hollohan (1992) is the leading case on the Tenth Schedule (anti-defection), not press privilege.
• Option (b): Correct — MSM Sharma vs. Sri Krishna Sinha (1959) was the first major Supreme Court case examining parliamentary privilege over press publications. The Supreme Court upheld the legislature's privilege, holding that the Bihar Legislative Assembly had the right to prohibit publication of expunged portions of its debates.
• Option (c): Incorrect — 'Searchlight case' is the popular name for the same controversy (named after the Searchlight newspaper involved), but the formal legal citation is MSM Sharma vs. Sri Krishna Sinha. The blank asks for the case name.
• Option (d): Incorrect — Raja Ram Pal vs. Speaker (2007) dealt with the cash-for-query expulsion cases, not the 1959 press publication dispute.

Value Addition:
• MSM Sharma (1959) established that courts can examine whether a privilege exists but cannot examine how Parliament exercised it.
• The case involved the Bihar Legislative Assembly, making it relevant to Article 194 (state legislature privileges) as well.
• The Searchlight newspaper controversy arose when the paper published portions of a speech that had been ordered expunged from the official record.

concepts_used: Privileges vs. Fundamental Rights: The Conflict and Resolution

solution.concept_anchor: Article 105 vs Part III — harmonious construction principle

statement_analysis.statement: Since Article 105 is itself a provision of the Constitution, parliamentary privileges operate as a constitutionally embedded exception to the fundamental rights guaranteed under Part III in the parliamentary context.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 105 is part of the constitutional text — it therefore operates at the same level as Part III rights, and courts apply harmonious construction to resolve conflicts rather than treating one as superior to the other.

statement_analysis.statement: The pre-Searchlight case legal position held that parliamentary privileges were superior to fundamental rights and courts could not interfere even if a fundamental right was being violated in the name of privilege.
statement_analysis.reason: Before the judicial evolution on this issue, the position was that privileges, being creatures of the Constitution, could not be challenged on the basis of fundamental rights — privileges were treated as paramount within their sphere.

statement_analysis.statement: Under the current legal framework, a member can invoke Article 19(1)(a) to challenge a parliamentary privilege rule that restricts what may be said in a committee proceeding, since Article 19 rights are universal and cannot be excluded by any other provision.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 105(1) speech immunity within Parliament is absolute and independent of Article 19 — conversely, restrictions within parliamentary proceedings are also governed by parliamentary privilege rules, not by Article 19(2). A member cannot challenge internal parliamentary restrictions using Article 19(1)(a).

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option d (all three) is a strong distractor because Statements 1 and 2 are both correct and sound authoritative, leading students to accept Statement 3 as equally sound — especially those who know Article 19(1)(a) applies broadly and miss the parliamentary context exception.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: Article 105 is a constitutional provision operating in the same tier as Part III — courts apply harmonious construction. This is correct.
Evaluate Statement 2: The pre-Searchlight position did treat privileges as superior — this accurately describes the historical legal position. Correct.

Evaluate Statement 3: The claim that Article 19(1)(a) can be used to challenge privilege-based restrictions on parliamentary speech is incorrect — Article 105 governs internal parliamentary speech entirely, independent of Article 19. Incorrect.
Statements 1 and 2 correct — select option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 3 is a partial-truth trap. It correctly identifies Article 19(1)(a) as a fundamental right and correctly notes that rights are important — but it misapplies the principle by extending Article 19(1)(a) into the sphere where Article 105 governs exclusively. The harmonious construction principle means neither provision completely destroys the other, but within Parliament, Article 105 governs speech, not Article 19. The inverted application of this principle is the trap.
solution.final_explanation:
The relationship between parliamentary privileges and fundamental rights has been a contested area of Indian constitutional law.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Article 105 is a constitutional provision. It therefore does not violate fundamental rights — it operates as a constitutionally authorized exception within the parliamentary sphere. Courts apply harmonious construction between Part III rights and Article 105.
• Statement 2 — Correct: The pre-Searchlight position treated privileges as paramount. Courts initially held that since privileges are constitutional, they cannot be challenged using fundamental rights — privileges were effectively superior in their domain.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: Article 19(1)(a) cannot be invoked to challenge restrictions within parliamentary proceedings. The constitutional scheme places speech within Parliament under Article 105(1), which is absolute and independent of Article 19. Similarly, privilege-based restrictions on what may be said or published are governed by privilege rules — Article 19 does not enter this domain.

Value Addition:
• The 'Special Reference under Article 143' case required the Supreme Court to opine on the interplay between privilege and fundamental rights, eventually leading to harmonious construction.
• Article 105(2) and Article 194(2) both protect publication of parliamentary reports made under the House's authority — creating an explicit Article 19 exception.
• The theoretical tension between privilege and fundamental rights remains unresolved in some edge cases.

concepts_used: Codification of Parliamentary Privileges: The Unresolved Constitutional Mandate

solution.concept_anchor: 44th Amendment 1978 — codification mandate unimplemented
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option c is a strong distractor because it inverts the actual state of affairs — students who know the 44th Amendment changed something about privilege may assume codification was completed, making option (c) sound like an accurate description of the current position.
elimination_logic: Eliminate option (b): The 42nd Amendment (1976) is associated with the Emergency-era changes — it did not specifically address parliamentary privilege codification.
Eliminate option (c): Codification has NOT been completed — the 44th Amendment mandated it but Parliament has not enacted the required law. This is a common misconception.
Eliminate option (d): There is no requirement in Article 105 for state legislatures' endorsement — the codification is Parliament's own responsibility under Article 105(3).
Confirm option (a): The 44th Amendment (1978) amended Article 105(3) to require Parliament to define privileges by law — but over 45 years later, no such law exists.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The temporal-swap trap exploits the gap between the 44th Amendment mandate (1978) and the present day. Students who know the 44th Amendment changed Article 105(3) may assume that the constitutional mandate has been fulfilled — that privileges were codified shortly after 1978. The fact that the mandate remains unfulfilled after 45+ years is one of the most commonly tested (and most commonly missed) facts in parliamentary privilege. Option (c) is designed to exploit this assumption directly.
solution.final_explanation:
Article 105(3) of the Constitution was amended by the 44th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1978 to require Parliament to define its privileges by law.

• Option (a): Correct — The 44th Amendment (1978) amended Article 105(3) but Parliament has never enacted the required law. As a result, the pre-Amendment default position — privileges co-extensive with the House of Commons as they stood at the Constitution's commencement — continues to apply.
• Option (b): Incorrect — The 42nd Amendment (1976) was the Emergency-era amendment that made sweeping changes to the Constitution, but it did not specifically address the codification of parliamentary privileges.
• Option (c): Incorrect — This inverts the actual legal position. The mandate exists; the fulfillment does not. Parliament has NOT codified its privileges despite the constitutional requirement.
• Option (d): Incorrect — Article 105(3) places the codification responsibility solely on Parliament. There is no requirement for any endorsement by state legislatures.

Value Addition:
• Arguments for codification: Legal certainty, preventing arbitrary use of privilege, transparency.
• Arguments against: Flexibility to respond to unforeseen situations; codification may inadvertently limit privileges.
• The same gap exists for state legislatures under Article 194(3) — state legislatures have also not codified their privileges.

solution.concept_anchor: Authorized vs unauthorized publication — contempt from selective misrepresentation
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option a is a strong distractor because a newspaper reporting parliamentary debates is indeed protected — students who stop at 'accurate reporting is protected' will not notice that selective quotation to misrepresent is contemplated in option (b) as the correct pair.
elimination_logic: Eliminate option (a): A newspaper that reports parliamentary debates accurately and completely is protected — this pair is correctly matched. Not the answer.

Evaluate option (b): A newspaper that accurately quotes individual statements but deliberately omits context to create a misleading impression is misrepresenting parliamentary proceedings — this constitutes contempt. This pair IS correctly matched and describes an important rule.

Eliminate option (c): The authorization of the House is required for absolute privilege to attach to publications — an unauthorized publication of secret session proceedings does NOT enjoy privilege. This pair is incorrectly matched.
Eliminate option (d): Expunged portions of debates are ordered removed from the official record — publishing them violates the House's authority and constitutes contempt, not a protected act.
Option (b) is the correctly matched pair.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Option (a) is the partial-truth trap — it describes a genuinely protected situation (accurate, fair reporting of debates is privileged), and students who correctly identify this may pick option (a) without reading option (b) carefully. Option (b) describes the nuanced rule that selective quotation designed to misrepresent is contempt even if each quoted statement is technically accurate — this is the more precise and UPSC-testable principle.
solution.final_explanation:
The protection available to publications of parliamentary proceedings depends critically on their authorization and accuracy.

• Option (a): Incorrect as the answer — but this pair is correctly matched. A newspaper accurately reporting parliamentary debates is protected by absolute privilege — no defamation suit lies. However, this is not the most precise answer.
• Option (b): Correct. This pair is correctly matched and identifies the contempt rule: selective quotation of parliamentary proceedings that, while accurate in parts, creates a false or misleading overall impression, constitutes contempt of Parliament. Accuracy of individual quotes does not provide immunity if the overall publication misrepresents the proceedings.
• Option (c): Incorrectly matched — unauthorized publication of secret session proceedings does NOT enjoy any privilege protection. Only authorized publications are absolutely privileged.
• Option (d): Incorrectly matched — publishing expunged portions of parliamentary debates is a contemptuous act, not a protected one. The expunction order removes those portions from the official record and prohibits their publication.

Value Addition:
• The MSM Sharma (1959) case directly involved unauthorized publication of expunged speech — the Supreme Court upheld the legislature's privilege.
• 'Fair and accurate' reporting is the twin test for press privilege in parliamentary reporting.
• Publication of a full and accurate report of any public sitting of either House is protected under the Parliamentary Proceedings (Protection of Publication) Act, 1977.

solution.concept_anchor: Kihoto Hollohan — anti-defection judicial review opposite to privilege decisions
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option a is a strong distractor because both A and R are correct and relate to the same constitutional domain (Speaker's powers), and the causal link between them seems obvious — students may not pause to verify whether the judicial review rule in anti-defection cases actually explains the Tenth Schedule classification.
elimination_logic: Step 1: Is Assertion (A) correct? — Yes. Under Kihoto Hollohan (1992), the Supreme Court held that the Speaker's decisions under the Tenth Schedule ARE subject to judicial review, unlike privilege decisions which are not reviewable under Article 122.
Step 2: Is Reason (R) correct? — Yes. The Tenth Schedule was inserted by the 52nd Constitutional Amendment (1985) — this is a correct factual statement.

Step 3: Does R causally explain A? — No. The fact that the Tenth Schedule was inserted by the 52nd Amendment does not explain why judicial review is available for anti-defection decisions. The reason for judicial review in Kihoto Hollohan was that the Speaker acts as a tribunal under the Tenth Schedule (exercising quasi-judicial power affecting fundamental rights of membership), not because of which amendment inserted the Schedule.
Both A and R are correct, but R does not explain A — select option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: This is a reversed-causation trap. The Reason correctly identifies the 52nd Amendment as the source of the Tenth Schedule. The Assertion correctly states that Kihoto Hollohan made anti-defection decisions judicially reviewable. But these two facts are not causally connected — the constitutional source of the Schedule does not determine reviewability. The actual reason for judicial review is the Speaker's quasi-judicial role affecting membership rights, not the amendment number. Students who verify both facts as true and stop there will incorrectly mark option (a).
solution.final_explanation:
The Tenth Schedule (anti-defection law) and parliamentary privilege represent two constitutionally distinct domains, and they have opposite positions on judicial review.

Assertion (A) — Correct: In Kihoto Hollohan vs. Zachillhu (1992), the Supreme Court held that the Speaker's decisions under the Tenth Schedule are subject to judicial review. This is the opposite of privilege decisions — where Article 122 bars judicial scrutiny. The reason is that the Speaker under the Tenth Schedule acts as a tribunal making quasi-judicial decisions that affect a member's fundamental right to hold public office.

Reason (R) — Correct: The Tenth Schedule was indeed inserted into the Constitution by the 52nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1985 — this is factually accurate.

Causal relationship: R does NOT explain A. The amendment that inserted the Tenth Schedule says nothing about judicial reviewability. The reviewability of anti-defection decisions was determined by the Speaker's quasi-judicial role and its impact on fundamental rights — not by which amendment created the Schedule.

Correct option: (b) — Both A and R correct, but R does not explain A.

Value Addition:
• Anti-defection decisions (judicially reviewable) vs. privilege decisions (not judicially reviewable) is a classic UPSC comparative trap.
• A party whip violation leading to anti-defection proceedings is governed by the Tenth Schedule — NOT by privilege law.
• The Speaker deciding on anti-defection is exercising a judicial function; the Speaker deciding on privilege is exercising a House management function.

concepts_used: Privileges of State Legislatures vs. Parliament: Similarities and Distinctions

solution.concept_anchor: State legislature privileges bounded by Parliament's privilege ceiling

statement_analysis.statement: Article 194 of the Constitution provides for privileges of state legislatures, and its structure mirrors Article 105 — state legislatures may claim any privilege that the Constitution does not explicitly deny them, including privileges beyond those enjoyed by Parliament.
statement_analysis.reason: State legislatures cannot claim privileges beyond what Parliament itself enjoys — their ceiling is Parliament's privilege level. A state legislature asserting a privilege not available to Parliament would be unconstitutional.

statement_analysis.statement: Since neither Parliament nor the state legislatures have codified their privileges by law, the position that both operate under is that privileges are co-extensive with those of the House of Commons as they existed at the Constitution's commencement.
statement_analysis.reason: Both Parliament (Article 105) and state legislatures (Article 194) face the same codification gap — neither has enacted the required law, so both default to the House of Commons position as of 1950.

statement_analysis.statement: A state legislature can create new privileges by simple resolution of the House, even if such privileges were not part of the House of Commons practice — this legislative autonomy is guaranteed by the federal structure under the Constitution.
statement_analysis.reason: State legislatures cannot expand their privileges through resolution — they are bound by the constitutional framework, and any privilege beyond what Parliament enjoys would be unconstitutional. Resolutions cannot create constitutional privileges.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Option c (statements 1 and 3 only) would be chosen by students who correctly identify Statement 1 as incorrect but mistakenly accept Statement 2 as incorrect as well, thinking the codification default rule is too simplistic to be correct.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: The claim that state legislatures can exceed Parliament's privilege level is incorrect — state legislature privileges are capped at Parliament's ceiling. Statement 1 IS incorrect.

Evaluate Statement 2: The codification default rule (House of Commons 1950 position) applies equally to both Parliament and state legislatures — Statement 2 is actually correct, so it does NOT belong in the 'incorrect' set.
Evaluate Statement 3: Simple resolutions cannot create constitutional privileges beyond established norms — this claim is incorrect. Statement 3 IS incorrect.
Statements 1 and 3 are incorrect — select option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 1 exploits the scope-extension trap by implying that the 'mirror' structure of Articles 105 and 194 means equal powers. The critical asymmetry is that state legislatures cannot exceed Parliament's privilege level — Articles 194 creates a parallel structure but not an equal ceiling. Statement 3 introduces a plausible-sounding 'legislative autonomy' principle that does not exist in privilege law — constitutional privileges cannot be created by mere resolution.
solution.final_explanation:
Article 194 creates a parallel privilege structure for state legislatures that mirrors Article 105 for Parliament. However, this mirroring comes with an important limitation.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: The 'mirror' structure does NOT mean equal powers without ceiling. State legislatures cannot claim privileges that Parliament itself does not enjoy. The constitutional architecture treats Parliament's privilege level as the maximum — any state legislature asserting a higher privilege crosses constitutional bounds.
• Statement 2 — Correct: The codification gap applies equally to both levels. Neither Parliament nor state legislatures have enacted the required definitional laws. Both therefore operate under the default: House of Commons privileges as they stood in 1950 at the Constitution's commencement.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: Constitutional privileges cannot be created or expanded through House resolutions. Resolutions are internal instruments — they can regulate procedure but cannot generate new constitutional privileges. The federal structure argument is irrelevant here — privilege law is constitutional, not federal-legislative.

Value Addition:
• State legislature privilege cases are argued under Article 194, which is structurally identical to Article 105 but subject to the Parliament-ceiling rule.
• MSM Sharma (1959) actually involved a state legislature (Bihar), making it relevant to Article 194 privilege jurisprudence.
• Both Articles 122 and 212 bar courts from questioning parliamentary and state legislature proceedings respectively.

solution.concept_anchor: Privilege motion admissibility conditions

statement_analysis.statement: A privilege motion must relate to the concerned member in their capacity as a member of the House — a grievance about something done by the member in a personal or non-parliamentary capacity is not admissible.
statement_analysis.reason: This is a well-established admissibility condition — the alleged breach must relate to the member's parliamentary role, not their personal conduct outside their parliamentary duties.

statement_analysis.statement: A privilege motion must be raised at the earliest opportunity after the alleged breach occurs — delay in raising the matter weakens its admissibility and the Speaker may reject it on this ground.
statement_analysis.reason: Timeliness is an admissibility condition — the member must raise the privilege matter at the first available opportunity; undue delay can be a ground for the Speaker to reject the motion.

statement_analysis.statement: If the matter that forms the basis of a privilege motion is already pending before a court of law, the Speaker must refuse admission to the privilege motion and refer the matter to the court for resolution.
statement_analysis.reason: If the matter is already before a court, the Speaker may refuse to admit the privilege motion — but there is no requirement to refer the matter to the court. The court-pending condition is a ground for rejection of the motion, not a trigger for mandatory referral.

statement_analysis.statement: A calling attention motion and a privilege motion serve the same constitutional purpose — both result in the same procedure before the Privileges Committee and carry identical consequences.
statement_analysis.reason: These are fundamentally different instruments: a calling attention motion draws the government's attention to an urgent matter of public importance; a privilege motion addresses breach of parliamentary privilege. Their procedures, purposes, and consequences are distinct.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Option c (Only three) tempts students who correctly identify Statements 1 and 2 as correct and then tentatively accept Statement 3 as correct because it sounds like a reasonable procedural safeguard against Parliament conflicting with courts.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: Relates-to-member-capacity requirement is a genuine admissibility condition. Correct.
Evaluate Statement 2: Earliest opportunity requirement is a well-established admissibility condition. Correct.
Evaluate Statement 3: The 'must refer to court' element is a fabrication — court-pending is a rejection ground but creates no obligation to refer. Incorrect.
Evaluate Statement 4: Calling attention motion ≠ privilege motion — different purposes, procedures, and consequences. Incorrect.
Only two statements (1 and 2) are correct — select option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 3 is a plausible-fabrication trap. The rule that a court-pending matter weakens a privilege motion's admissibility is real — but the added claim that the Speaker 'must refer to court' is invented. The Speaker's correct action is to reject the privilege motion, not to act as a referral conduit to the judiciary. Students who know the court-pending rule but are uncertain about its procedural consequence will accept the fabricated referral obligation.
solution.final_explanation:
Privilege motion admissibility depends on satisfying specific conditions that ensure the motion addresses genuine parliamentary concerns rather than political tactics.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The alleged breach must relate to the member in their parliamentary capacity. Personal grievances or extra-parliamentary conduct do not qualify.
• Statement 2 — Correct: Timeliness is a core admissibility condition. The member must raise the matter at the earliest opportunity. The Speaker applies this standard rigorously — belated motions are routinely rejected.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: When a matter is already before a court, the Speaker may decline to admit the privilege motion (to avoid concurrent proceedings). However, there is no obligation to 'refer' the matter to court — the court already has it. The rejection ground and the mandatory referral obligation are very different propositions.
• Statement 4 — Incorrect: A calling attention motion and a privilege motion are entirely different parliamentary instruments. A calling attention motion seeks government's attention to urgent public matters. A privilege motion addresses breach of parliamentary privilege. Their admissibility criteria, procedures, and consequences differ substantially.

Value Addition:
• The Speaker's decision on admissibility of a privilege motion is final and not subject to judicial review under Article 122.
• In practice, many privilege motions are rejected at the prima facie stage — the Committee rarely completes full proceedings.
• Recent years have seen a sharp rise in privilege motions used as political pressure tools rather than genuine privilege complaints.

solution.concept_anchor: Post-Sita Soren bribery outside parliamentary immunity — CBI investigation valid
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option a is a strong distractor because students who know Article 105(1) broadly may assume any investigation touching a member's voting behaviour falls within the immunity zone — missing the post-Sita Soren distinction between the corrupt act and the parliamentary act.
elimination_logic: Identify the legal event: Post-2024 Sita Soren ruling, bribery of a legislator is no longer shielded by parliamentary privilege — the act of accepting a bribe is outside Parliament, even if the vote is cast inside.

Eliminate option (a): Investigative agencies cannot be barred from investigating bribery under Article 105 post-Sita Soren — the immunity covers the parliamentary act (voting), not the corrupt transaction (bribe acceptance).

Eliminate option (b): The investigation does not require Speaker's prior approval — the Sita Soren ruling did not create a new procedural requirement of Speaker's permission for bribery investigations.

Eliminate option (d): The Member does not enjoy immunity from investigation merely because no-confidence vote proceedings are privileged — the bribery transaction remains outside privilege even if the vote itself is protected.

Confirm option (c): Under the current legal position (post-Sita Soren, 2024), the CBI can investigate bribe acceptance — the act of receiving money is outside Parliament and is not covered by Article 105(1) immunity.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Option (a) is a partial-truth trap. It correctly identifies Article 105(1) as the immunity provision but incorrectly extends it to cover the entire transaction including bribe acceptance. Post-Sita Soren, the Supreme Court drew a clear line: the privilege covers the parliamentary act (casting the vote); it does not cover the corrupt transaction (accepting the bribe), which occurs outside Parliament. Students who know the pre-2024 position (PV Narasimha Rao) will select option (a), missing the landmark 2024 overruling.
solution.final_explanation:
This scenario tests the application of the Sita Soren (2024) ruling, which fundamentally changed the legal position on legislative bribery.

Applicable principle: In Sita Soren vs. Union of India (2024), the Supreme Court unanimously held that a legislator who accepts a bribe to vote in a particular manner in the House is NOT protected by parliamentary privilege. The privilege under Article 105(1) protects the act of voting — it does not extend to the preceding act of accepting money, which is a criminal transaction occurring outside Parliament.

Mapping to the scenario: The MP allegedly received money before casting the vote in the no-confidence motion. The bribe acceptance is the actus reus of the crime — it occurred outside Parliament. The CBI's investigation concerns this criminal transaction.

• Option (a): Incorrect. Post-Sita Soren, Article 105(1) does not shield bribery — the investigation is not barred.
• Option (b): Incorrect. The Sita Soren ruling did not create any requirement for the Speaker's prior sanction before investigating legislative bribery. No such procedural safeguard exists in law.
• Option (c): Correct. The CBI may lawfully investigate bribe acceptance — the criminal transaction falls outside parliamentary privilege.
• Option (d): Incorrect. The privilege attaches to the vote cast inside Parliament, not to the bribery transaction — the two are constitutionally distinct under current law.

Value Addition:
• Sita Soren (2024) explicitly overruled PV Narasimha Rao (1998) — students must know the current legal position.
• The constitutional rationale: privilege protects Parliament's functioning; shielding corruption undermines that very functioning.
• Post-2024, MPs can face full investigation and prosecution for bribery without any parliamentary immunity defence.

solution.concept_anchor: Private individual contempt — strangers can be punished

statement_analysis.statement: Parliamentary privileges belong primarily to the House as a body, individual members, and certain officers — private citizens and visitors cannot be punished by Parliament even if their conduct obstructs parliamentary business.
statement_analysis.reason: Parliament can punish private individuals (strangers) for contempt — a non-member who obstructs parliamentary business or brings the House into disrepute can be summoned and punished. Privileges are not limited in their protective application to members alone.

statement_analysis.statement: Journalists reporting parliamentary proceedings are protected against legal proceedings when their reporting is fair and accurate, but the House retains the authority to prohibit publication of its proceedings entirely.
statement_analysis.reason: Fair and accurate reporting enjoys protection, but this is conditional — the House can order that proceedings not be published (as in secret sittings), overriding even the general press freedom to report.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option a (both correct) attracts students who focus on the second half of Statement 1 ('privileges belong to the House...') and accept it superficially without noticing the false conclusion ('cannot be punished') appended to it.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: The opening characterization (privileges belong primarily to the House, members, officers) is partially accurate — but the conclusion (private citizens CANNOT be punished) is false. Non-members can be and are punished for contempt. Statement 1 is incorrect.
Evaluate Statement 2: Both parts of Statement 2 are accurate — fair and accurate press reporting is protected; the House can also prohibit publication. Statement 2 is correct.
Statement 1 incorrect, Statement 2 correct — select option (d).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 1 is a scope-extension trap with a partial-truth wrapper. The opening clause about privileges 'belonging primarily' to the House and members is accurate — but the extension 'therefore private citizens cannot be punished' is false. Parliament has contempt powers that extend to non-members. The trap works because students accept the accurate opening and do not critically examine the conclusion it is used to support.
solution.final_explanation:
Parliamentary privileges operate both as protections for members and as powers of the House against those who obstruct or disrespect it.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: While it is true that privileges primarily protect the House, its members, and officers, this does not mean private individuals are exempt from parliamentary sanction. A stranger (visitor, lobbyist, journalist, or any private person) who obstructs parliamentary business, creates a disturbance, or brings the House into disrepute can be summoned and punished for contempt. Parliament's contempt power is wide and applies to non-members.
• Statement 2 — Correct: Journalists reporting parliamentary debates are protected when the reporting is fair and accurate. However, this protection is conditional — the House has the overriding authority to prohibit publication of its proceedings (as in secret sittings). When such prohibition is in place, even accurate reporting becomes contempt.

Value Addition:
• A private person who assaults or threatens a member in connection with their parliamentary role can be punished for contempt by Parliament.
• The Parliamentary Proceedings (Protection of Publication) Act, 1977 specifically protects newspapers from defamation suits for accurately publishing parliamentary proceedings.
• During secret sittings, the prohibition on publication overrides all press freedom considerations.

solution.concept_anchor: 40-day civil arrest immunity — session plus 40 days before and after
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option c (30 days) is a strong distractor because students who vaguely recall a 'month-based' protection period may approximate to 30 days, confusing it with other legislative time periods such as the 30-day period for Parliamentary approval of Ordinances.
elimination_logic: Eliminate option (a): 15 days corresponds to no parliamentary protection period — it is too short and not a recognized parliamentary privilege time frame.
Eliminate option (c): 30 days is associated with other parliamentary time periods (Ordinance laying requirements) — it is not the civil arrest immunity window.
Eliminate option (d): 60 days would extend protection significantly beyond what the established rule provides — no such duration exists in parliamentary practice.
Confirm option (b): The freedom from civil arrest privilege covers the session + 40 days before + 40 days after the session — 40 days is the correct number.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The temporal-swap trap targets candidates who know a 'days before/after session' rule exists but cannot recall the exact number. UPSC exploits this by offering 30 days (associated with Ordinance approval) and 60 days (plausible longer window) as near-correct options. The answer — 40 days — must be memorized precisely, as the distinction from 30 or 60 days is a frequently tested point in parliamentary privilege questions.
solution.final_explanation:
Freedom from arrest in civil cases is a specific parliamentary privilege that creates a protected window around parliamentary sessions.

• Option (a): Incorrect — 15 days corresponds to no recognized parliamentary privilege window. It is too short to be operationally meaningful.
• Option (b): Correct — Members of Parliament are immune from arrest in civil cases during the session of the House AND for 40 days before and after the session. An arrest made within this window is void. This protection does NOT cover criminal cases or preventive detention.
• Option (c): Incorrect — 30 days is associated with the period within which an Ordinance must be laid before Parliament and various committee timelines, not the civil arrest immunity window.
• Option (d): Incorrect — 60 days does not correspond to any parliamentary privilege time frame — it is a plausible but fabricated duration.

Value Addition:
• The total protected window (40 days before + session + 40 days after) means members effectively enjoy civil arrest immunity for most of the year if sessions are frequent.
• Upon any arrest (even of a non-member related to parliamentary business), the arresting authority must notify the Speaker/Chairman.
• This 40-day rule applies only to civil suits — a member accused in a criminal case enjoys no such immunity and can be arrested and detained.
